analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% surtax on individual income above the multi-million-dollar level.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2026 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has had no further action; it has a sponsor and 9 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The Millionaires Surtax Act would add a 10% tax on each dollar of income above $2 million for married couples and $1 million for everyone else, on top of existing taxes. It applies to all types of income, including investment gains, though taxpayers could still subtract their investment interest deductions. It would take effect for tax years starting after December 31, 2026, and the money would go into the general Treasury rather than to any specific program.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the general public would gain through new federal revenue paid exclusively by households earning over $1 million ($2 million for joint filers) — a group of roughly the top fraction of one percent of taxpayers. That money could fund public priorities or reduce deficits, though the bill itself does not dedicate it to anything. Middle- and lower-income households would owe nothing new under this bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The general public, via new revenue

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 10% surtax on modified adjusted gross income above $2 million for joint filers and $1 million for other taxpayers, so only the highest-income households pay it.
The surtax applies to all income — including capital gains and investment income — rather than only wages, so high earners cannot avoid it by shifting pay into investment income.
The tax would begin with tax years after December 31, 2026, and the revenue it raises would flow to the Treasury for general federal use.

analysis.who_pays: Households with income over $2 million (joint) or $1 million (single and other filers) would pay 10 cents of every dollar above those thresholds, in addition to their existing federal taxes. Estates and trusts with high income are also covered. No other taxpayers would pay anything under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue but does not dedicate it to any program or tax cut, so ordinary people get no guaranteed direct benefit — the money simply enters the general Treasury.

It leaves the investment interest deduction intact, so wealthy investors who borrow heavily to finance investments can shield part of their income from the surtax, which favors leveraged investors over those earning wages.
The $1 million and $2 million thresholds are not indexed to inflation, so over time the tax would reach more taxpayers as incomes rise.

It adds a new layer on top of the existing tax code rather than closing loopholes like the carried-interest treatment that lets fund managers pay lower rates, so it does not simplify the system it taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: a large new stream of revenue drawn only from households above $1 million in income, with no effect on anyone earning less. The cost to those taxpayers is real but proportionate — 10% of income above the threshold — and a good-faith objection is that the bill does nothing to direct the money to visible public benefits or to fix the underlying loopholes that let some very high earners pay lower effective rates. As designed it is a clean, targeted revenue measure, not comprehensive tax reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and no committee vote or floor action has happened yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act on April 15, 2026, with five original cosponsors: Reps. Cohen, Deluzio, Norton, Tlaib, and Davis of Illinois.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation.
Nine additional members had signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats, and the bill has had no committee markup, vote, or floor action since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete — the bill is sitting in committee. High-income households are spared any new tax as long as it does not advance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; the bill sits in committee

industries.note: These taxpayers would owe an extra 10% on every dollar of income above $2 million (joint) or $1 million (other filers), including investment income. Their saving grace is that investment interest remains deductible for surtax purposes.

industries.industry: Hedge funds, private equity, and investment managers
industries.note: Fund managers routinely earn over $1 million, much of it as investment income, so the surtax would reach carried interest and fund profits that currently enjoy lower rates. It does not eliminate the carried-interest break, but it adds a layer of tax on top of it.
A new surtax with special rules for nonresident aliens, expatriates, trusts, and estates creates additional tax preparation and planning work for high-income clients.

analysis.trajectory: A tax bill from a minority-party member with 9 cosponsors rarely reaches the floor. It will most likely stay in the Ways and Means Committee without a markup or vote unless tax legislation moves through the committee and a member attaches it as an amendment; the most realistic outcome is that it dies quietly when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
